scenario.name: Microsoft Threat Intel — Midnight Blizzard (APT29): OAuth App Persistence & EWS Exfiltration
scenario.shortSubtitle: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · Legacy Tenant Password Spray, OAuth full_access_as_app & EWS
scenario.overview: Imagine a patient espionage crew softly trying one spare key per evening from scattered neighborhood cars against a forgotten backyard testing shed that never got a modern two-factor deadbolt. Once inside the dusty shed, they discover an old cross-campus courier badge that was accidentally left with master mailroom powers, use it to print brand-new official courier badges inside the corporate headquarters, and silently haul out executive mailbags through the automated mail chute. In this scenario (T1098.003, Microsoft Threat Intel, Midnight Blizzard (APT29): OAuth App Persistence & EWS Exfiltration), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: low-Volume Residential-Proxy Password Spray, then abusing a Legacy Cross-Tenant OAuth App, then exfiltrating Corporate Mailboxes. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Low-Volume Residential-Proxy Password Spray, then Abusing a Legacy Cross-Tenant OAuth App, then Exfiltrating Corporate Mailboxes, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: LOW-VOLUME PASSWORD SPRAY ON LEGACY TEST TENANT
stages.subtitle: Compromising non-production account lacking MFA via residential proxies
stages.description: Avoiding noisy repeated knocks that would wake the guard dogs, the spy crew tries only a handful of common passwords slowly across hundreds of ordinary household street addresses until a forgotten back-lot testing shed with no second-factor padlock quietly clicks open. To avoid triggering automated IP blocks or account lockouts, the attacker routes authentication requests through a rotating pool of residential proxy IPs (home internet routers in the same country as the target, making login traffic look like legitimate local employees rather than a datacenter botnet) and performs a low-volume password spray (trying just one common password at a time across a small list of accounts) against a forgotten, non-production legacy test tenant account that had never been enforced with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA). Because each residential proxy IP sends only a tiny fraction of the total login attempts and stays well below the bad-password lockout threshold (e.g., 1 attempt per hour), traditional velocity-based brute-force rules do not fire, allowing the attacker to quietly log into the forgotten single-factor test account. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LEGACY TENANT SPRAY / ⇠#1 RESP ResultType 0) from Node ① (#1 Midnight Blizzard Proxy Pool) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & Defender XDR).

stages.title: MALICIOUS OAUTH APP REGISTRATION & ROLE CONSENT
stages.subtitle: Abusing legacy test OAuth app to grant full_access_as_app in Exchange
stages.description: Rummaging inside the unlocked testing shed, the spies uncover an abandoned automated courier badge that still carries wide building-wide authority into the main corporate tower, and immediately use it to mint shiny new official machine badges armed with full mailroom keys. Inside the test environment, the attacker discovers a legacy OAuth test application whose Service Principal had been granted privileged directory permissions, specifically AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All (a high-privilege Microsoft Graph permission that allows an app to grant any permission role to itself or to other apps without asking a human Global Administrator), inside the main corporate tenant. Using that legacy app, the attacker creates new malicious OAuth Service Principals, attaches new client secret keys (Add servicePrincipal credentials, creating long-lived API passwords for the app), and assigns them the Office 365 Exchange Online full_access_as_app role. In Microsoft Entra ID, an application holding AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All can call the Graph API (/servicePrincipals/{id}/appRoleAssignments) to self-assign full_access_as_app (Role ID dc890d15-9560-4a4c-9b7f-a736ec74ec40, the highest application-level Exchange permission), escalating from a forgotten test account to full tenant-wide mail access without touching a human admin’s account. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ GRANT FULL_ACCESS_AS_APP / ⇠#2 RESP Role Granted) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Microsoft Entra ID Control Plane), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & Defender XDR).

stages.title: OAUTH BEARER TOKEN EWS MAILBOX EXFILTRATION
stages.subtitle: Querying outlook.office365.com/EWS/Exchange.asmx via residential proxies
stages.description: Presenting their freshly minted machine-only courier badge straight at the automated postal bay, the spies bypass human lobby guards altogether and quietly wheel out corporate leadership correspondence without ever triggering a human sign-in prompt. Authenticating purely as the rogue OAuth application using grant_type=client_credentials (machine-to-machine authentication that uses the app’s client secret and never involves a human user login or MFA prompt), the attacker calls Exchange Web Services (https://outlook.office365.com/EWS/Exchange.asmx) through the same residential proxy pool to search and download emails from senior executive and security-team mailboxes. Because full_access_as_app is an application-level permission (Application Permission) rather than a delegated user permission (Delegated Permission), the OAuth Bearer token grants direct read/export access to any mailbox in the Exchange Online tenant without ever logging in as those users or triggering Conditional Access user-MFA policies. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ EWS MAIL EXFIL / ⇠#3 RESP 412 Items) from Node ③ (#3 Microsoft Entra ID Control Plane) to Node ④ (#4 Malicious OAuth Service Principal), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & Defender XDR).

detectionRule.title: Single-Factor Sign-In to Legacy or Test Tenant Accounts
detectionRule.ruleCode:
SigninLogs
| where ResultType == 0 and AuthenticationRequirement == "singleFactorAuthentication"
| where UserPrincipalName has_any ("test", "legacy", "svc")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ConditionalAccessStatus
detectionRule.mitigation: Decommission unused legacy tenants/accounts and enforce Conditional Access with phishing-resistant MFA across 100% of accounts and service principals.

detectionRule.title: Microsoft Threat Intel — OAuth App Assigned Exchange full_access_as_app
detectionRule.ruleCode:
AuditLogs
| where OperationName == "Add app role assignment to service principal"
| mv-expand TargetResources
| mv-expand TargetResources.modifiedProperties
| where tostring(TargetResources_modifiedProperties.newValue) has_any ("dc890d15-9560-4a4c-9b7f-a736ec74ec40", "full_access_as_app", "Mail.ReadWrite")
detectionRule.mitigation: Audit all OAuth service principals holding Application.ReadWrite.All or AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All and replace EWS full_access_as_app with scoped RBAC for Applications.

detectionRule.title: Anomalous EWS MailItemsAccessed by Newly Registered OAuth AppId
detectionRule.ruleCode:
CloudAppEvents
| where ActionType == "MailItemsAccessed"
| where RawEventData.ClientInfoString has "Client=WebServices"
| summarize AccessedCount = count() by tostring(RawEventData.AppId), IPAddress
| where AccessedCount > 100
detectionRule.mitigation: Disable legacy Exchange Web Services (EWS) application impersonation where unneeded and enforce Workload Identity Conditional Access policies.
